analysis.one_liner: Treats super PAC spending coordinated with candidates as campaign contributions and bars candidates from fundraising for super PACs.
analysis.headline: Backed by 9 House Democrats and no Republicans, the bill has sat in the House Administration Committee without a hearing or vote since its introduction in September 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat money that super PACs and other outside groups spend "in coordination" with a candidate as a campaign contribution to that candidate — meaning it would count against contribution limits, have to be disclosed, and trigger penalties if the limits are exceeded. It spells out what counts as coordination: shared campaign consultants, help raising money, candidate family involvement, or republishing campaign material, and it explicitly says setting up internal "firewalls" is no defense. It would also bar federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting or directing money to super PACs and similar committees that accept unlimited donations.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters get more disclosure and a clearer rule that outside money which is secretly coordinated with a campaign is limited and reportable, just like direct donations. Candidates who rely on small donors rather than super PAC money compete on a more level field, because rivals can no longer legally outsource big spending to friendly outside groups. Small donors and rank-and-file citizens gain influence relative to million-dollar donors, since the huge checks that fuel coordinated super PAC spending would carry legal consequences.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, and candidates without super PAC backing

how_it_helps.text: Payments for coordinated expenditures by outside groups would count as contributions to the candidate, so they would be subject to contribution limits and to disclosure and reporting requirements.

The bill defines coordination to include money raised or spent by groups formed at a candidate's urging, groups whose consultants also work for the campaign, groups the candidate fundraises for, and groups run by the candidate's family — and it expressly rejects the 'firewall' defense, so a shared operative is coordination even if the group claims internal walls.

Federal candidates and officeholders would be prohibited from soliciting, receiving, directing, or transferring funds to super PACs or 527 groups that accept donations outside the normal limits — closing the common practice of politicians headlining super PAC fundraisers.

Penalties are concrete: someone who knowingly and willfully makes an unlawful coordinated payment can be fined 300% of the amount over the limit, and officers, directors, and managers are personally on the hook if the organization doesn't pay.

The bill repeals the FEC's existing coordination regulations and requires new ones that match the stricter statutory standard, with the new rules applying even if the FEC misses its own deadline to write them.

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs, mega-donors, and outside groups would lose the ability to spend without limit in coordination with candidates. Political consultants and media firms that work for both a campaign and an outside group would have to pick one side. Candidates would lose their easiest route to big-money support and would have to fundraise within the normal limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs, mega-donors, and shared consultants

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad and could catch groups that are genuinely independent in fact: hiring a consultant who once worked for a campaign, officers having more than incidental talks with a candidate's family member, or a candidate appearing at the group's fundraiser can all make spending 'coordinated' even without any joint work on ads.

The bill says a group cannot defend itself by showing it used a firewall to keep its staff separate from the campaign, which removes the main structural safeguard careful organizations currently rely on.

It repeals the FEC's current coordination rules 90 days after enactment and applies the new standard 120 days after enactment whether or not the FEC has written replacement regulations, creating a window of legal uncertainty for groups trying to comply.
Enforcement depends on proving a knowing and willful violation before the FEC and courts, so in practice the stiff 300% penalty may reach only the most blatant cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — coordinated super PAC money should be treated like a contribution, not disguised as independent speech — addresses a well-documented loophole, and the joint personal liability for officers gives the rule teeth. The trade-off is overbreadth: the shared-consultant, family, and no-firewall provisions could chill lawful issue groups and force consultants out of one side of a race, and the transition period without FEC rules adds confusion. The bill would benefit from tighter lines around indirect ties, but the direction is sound.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the bill on September 9, 2025, joined by Reps. Mullin and Tlaib as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration, which has jurisdiction over election law.
Eight additional members have cosponsored, all Democrats, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, super PACs, mega-donors, and candidates who rely on coordinated outside spending are better off: the current rules allowing unlimited outside spending with loose coordination standards remain untouched, since the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Super PACs and big donors, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 9 backers are House Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee that has not acted on it.

industries.industry: Super PACs and big-money outside spending groups
industries.note: Their core product — unlimited spending that is quietly coordinated with campaigns — would become a limited, reportable contribution, and candidates could no longer headline their fundraisers. That money currently shapes which candidates can compete, which is why the bill targets it.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign media firms
industries.note: The shared-vendor rule would force consultants and media buyers to choose between campaign clients and outside-group clients, since serving both would make the outside group's spending a coordinated contribution with personal liability attached for officers.

The ban on candidate and officeholder fundraising would extend beyond super PACs to 527 groups accepting unlimited donations, cutting off a channel that currently moves large, undisclosed sums with politicians' active help.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship, no hearing scheduled, and a Republican-chaired committee in a Republican-led House, the most likely path is that the bill sits without action and quietly expires when this Congress ends in January 2027, as most private-member campaign finance bills do.
